newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Former ministers denied access to ousted Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: Former ministers denied access to ousted Bhutto.

text.p: Pakistani police prevented ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto from receiving visits from her former cabinet colleagues on Tuesday, ex-ministers said.
Former science and technology minister Nawaz Khokhar told Reuters Bhutto was apparently being kept at the prime minister's house and had been denied contact with her old colleagues.
He said several ex-ministers had tried in vain to see her after President Farooq Leghari dismissed her three-year-old government overnight, citing corruption and other abuses.

"We have looked for her everywhere," Khokhar said, adding that police had stopped him and other former ministers at a checkpoint about one km (half a mile) from her official residence, on a low hill overlooking a complex of government buildings.
"All the telephones of the prime minister's house have been disconnected and we have no information about her," he said. "She is not even at her private residence (in Islamabad)."

Khokhar, a former opposition member who faced criminal charges before changing his loyalties to join Bhutto's cabinet, said there was no word on the whereabouts of Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari, detained by troops in Lahore before dawn.

Troops moved into the capital Islamabad in the early hours to guard key installations, but stayed off the streets, which remained calm, apart from a few fire-crackers let off by celebrating shopkeepers. Schools and businesses opened as usual.
Leghari named veteran politician Meraj Khalid, once a Bhutto loyalist, as caretaker prime minister to supervise general elections he set for February 3, 1997.

Former parliamentary affairs minister Sher Afghan Niazi said courts had in the past not looked favourably on previous presidential dismissals of elected governments under the constitutional article invoked by Leghari.
"Dismissals under this article have never been held up by the courts in the past," Niazi told Reuters.
He said Bhutto and her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) colleagues had not decided whether to challenge Leghari's order in court. "It is up to the party leader to decide," he said.
Former minister for political and religious affairs Jehangir Badr said the PPP's central executive committee was expected to meet on Wednesday to decide its strategy.
